sources.title: Chao (2001): the fishery, diversity and conservation of ornamental fishes in the Rio Negro basin, a review of Project Piaba
sources.supports: water level at Barcelos (gauge, 1967-98): high June to August, low "usually from December to March"; monthly levels in 1998/99 peak in July (905 cm) and bottom in November and December (313-315 cm), and in 1995/96 are lowest October to December. The game reads this as rising January to May, high June to August, falling in September, low October to December

designNotes: Placed in an archipelago lake (checklist codes B and C); the checklist records it in habitats BDF. Month curve: more often met as the water drops and fish crowd into lagoons, beaches and rapids, fewer at high water when they spread into the forest. A game reading of the flood pulse, not a measured catch rate. Occurrence pass: month curve moved one month later to the Barcelos gauge calendar (Chao 2001).

sources.title: Chao (2001): the fishery, diversity and conservation of ornamental fishes in the Rio Negro basin, a review of Project Piaba
sources.supports: the ornamental (cardinal tetra) fishing season at Barcelos coincides with low water, October to February (also given as October to April); shipments peaked in November and February in 1995/96

designNotes: Placed in a forest stream (checklist code E); the checklist records it in habitats DE. Scooped with a dip net from the stream that feeds the lagoon, as the piabeiros of Barcelos do. Real cardinal fishing follows the flood (they live in streams and flooded margins); here the stream is fished all year. Occurrence pass: net catches follow the piabeiros' season at low water, October to February; scarce at high water when the fish spread into the forest.

designNotes: Added on 28 November 2026. Placed in the open lagoon over a muddy bottom (checklist code B; FishBase: adults over mud in lakes). A field study caught 63% of them by day and 27% at night (Saint-Paul et al. 2000, via Animal Diversity Web), so day leans slightly higher.
